content: Nephrolithiasis, also known as urinary stone disease, is a condition in children that leads to significant health issues and is becoming more common in North America. As a result, medical and dietary interventions (MDI) aimed at preventing recurrent urinary stones in children are gaining importance in clinical practice. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of medical and dietary interventions for preventing idiopathic urinary stones in children aged 1 to 18 years. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, the International Clinical Trials Register (ICTRP), and ClinicalTrials.gov. The search also included handsearching renal-related journals and conference proceedings, as well as reviewing weekly alerts from selected renal journals. The final search was completed on February 14, 2017, and no language restrictions were applied. The study included randomized controlled trials lasting at least one year that compared MDI to a control group for the prevention of recurrent idiopathic (non-syndromic) nephrolithiasis in children. Standard Cochrane methodologies were used for data collection and analysis, including screening titles and abstracts for relevance, extracting data, assessing risk of bias, and evaluating the quality of evidence using the GRADE approach. The search identified one relevant study involving 125 children (72 boys and 53 girls) with calcium-containing idiopathic nephrolithiasis and normal kidney structure. These children had undergone initial treatment with shockwave lithotripsy (SWL). Participants were randomized to receive either oral potassium citrate at a dose of 1 mEq/kg per day for 12 months or no specific medication or preventive measures. Results were reported for 96 children (48 in each group), including those who were stone-free (n = 52) and those with residual stone fragments (n = 44) after SWL. The primary outcomes showed that medical therapy with potassium citrate may reduce the recurrence of urinary stones. The risk ratio (RR) for stone recurrence was 0.19 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.06 to 0.60), which corresponds to 270 fewer stone recurrences per 1000 children (ranging from 133 to 313 fewer). However, the quality of evidence was downgraded by two levels due to significant study limitations, including unclear allocation concealment (selection bias) and high risks of performance, detection, and attrition bias. Adverse events were incompletely reported, but six out of 48 children (12.5%) receiving potassium citrate discontinued the trial due to side effects. This corresponds to a RR of 13.0 (95% CI 0.75 to 224.53), but the quality of evidence was very low due to study limitations and imprecision. An absolute effect size estimate could not be calculated. No data were available on retreatment rates. For secondary outcomes, no evidence was found regarding changes in serum electrolytes, 24-hour urine parameters, or the time to new stone formation. Preplanned secondary analyses could not be performed due to insufficient data. In conclusion, oral potassium citrate supplementation may reduce the recurrence of calcium-containing urinary stones in children following SWL. However, the confidence in this finding is limited due to the low quality of evidence. A significant proportion of children discontinued the medication due to adverse effects. There is no available trial evidence on retreatment rates. Further well-designed clinical trials are urgently needed to address these gaps in knowledge and improve the management of nephrolithiasis in children.
